title: QuantaPay x Redwood — POC scoping (Dedicated benchmark + traffic replay)
next_steps: Redwood to send POC plan doc + benchmark template (inputs/outputs, metrics definitions) by EOD Fri
QuantaPay to provide a sanitized request log sample (prompt + params + response length distribution) and target concurrency by Mon
Schedule a 60-min technical working session to align on traffic replay harness and success criteria (Markus/Simran + Elena/Chris)
Redwood to provision Dedicated sandbox endpoint (region: us-east preferred) with agreed model(s) and a fixed commit window for the benchmark week
Priyom to share a draft case study participation outline and conditional approval language (only publish if targets met + customer signoff)
body:
Meeting Header
Date: May 22, 2025
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 53 min
Meeting name: QuantaPay x Redwood — POC scoping (Dedicated benchmark + traffic replay)

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Priyom Das (AE), Markus Klein (Dir SE), Simran Kaur (Solutions Architect)
QuantaPay: Nadia Patel, Chris Dwyer, Elena Rossi, Samir Khan

Summary (auto)
- Team aligned on running a 2-week POC focused on predictable p95 latency, throughput under burst, and error rate under load.
- Agreed to use a traffic replay approach with a sanitized request set that preserves length + tool-calling mix.
- Success criteria drafted: p95 latency threshold at target concurrency, <0.5% 5xx/timeouts, and stable performance during 30–60 min sustained runs.
- QuantaPay open to a public case study if acceptance thresholds are met and claims are scoped to the benchmark window / workload.

Topics (auto)
- Workload and request shape
- Dedicated capacity sizing + burst behavior
- Benchmark harness and traffic replay
- Metrics + acceptance thresholds
- Security/logging constraints for test
- Case study / reference call conditional agreement

Action items (auto)
- Redwood: send POC plan + checklist, include how to compute p50/p95, error definitions, and cost-per-1k tokens
- QuantaPay: provide sanitized prompts + parameter distribution + expected RPS/concurrency
- Schedule technical working session for harness alignment


Transcript

[00:00] Priyom Das: Cool, I think we’re all here. Thanks everyone for making time. Goal today is just to scope the POC in a way where if it’s successful, it’s obvious, right? Like we’re not debating numbers at the end.

[00:15] Nadia Patel: Yep. That’s exactly what we want. We’ve been burned by “it depends” benchmarks.

[00:20] Markus Klein: Totally. We’ll write down the metrics, the measurement window, and the load shape, so we’re comparing apples to apples.

[00:29] Simran Kaur: And we’ll also be clear what’s in and out. Like, if you want tool calling in the loop, or if you want pure generation.

[00:36] Elena Rossi: For us it’s mostly generation but we do have a structured output mode, like JSON, and occasionally a function call. Not always.

[00:44] Chris Dwyer: And the big thing is we can’t have latency spikes when concurrency ramps. The average looks fine but the p95 kills us.

[00:52] Priyom Das: Got it. Maybe start with a quick recap of the workflow. Nadia, can you describe what the model is doing in prod? Just high level.

[01:02] Nadia Patel: Sure. We’re using an LLM to assist risk reviewers—so it summarizes transaction context, flags anomalies, and drafts a rationale. It’s not customer-facing, but it’s on the critical path for our ops team. If it’s slow, our queue backs up.

[01:19] Samir Khan: And we have internal SLOs: the UI needs something streaming quickly, but the full response needs to land in a reasonable time, otherwise they just skip using it.

[01:30] Markus Klein: Okay, so streaming time-to-first-token matters, plus the full completion latency.

[01:36] Elena Rossi: Exactly. Most prompts are like, I don’t know, 800 to 2k tokens input. Output varies—sometimes 200 tokens, sometimes 800.

[01:48] Simran Kaur: Helpful. Do you have a rough distribution? Even buckets are fine.

[01:54] Elena Rossi: I can pull percentiles. We do log prompt length and completion length. We’ll need to sanitize content, but the lengths we can keep.

[02:03] Chris Dwyer: Also concurrency. We get bursts at shift changes. It can go from like 10 concurrent to 60 concurrent in a couple minutes.

[02:13] Priyom Das: Perfect, that gives us a way to design the load test.

[02:18] Markus Klein: Let’s talk POC structure. We usually do two phases: (1) functional integration, (2) benchmark week where we lock config and run repeated tests.

[02:30] Nadia Patel: What’s typical timeline?

[02:32] Priyom Das: Two weeks is normal. Week one integration and baseline, week two is the formal measurement window.

[02:39] Chris Dwyer: We can do two weeks if we have an endpoint quickly.

[02:43] Priyom Das: For QuantaPay we’re assuming Dedicated. That means we’ll allocate a reserved pool, and you’re not fighting noisy neighbors.

[02:52] Nadia Patel: Dedicated is what we want to evaluate, yes.

[02:56] Markus Klein: So from a scoping standpoint, we need three things from you: request shapes, target concurrency/RPS, and the success criteria.

[03:06] Elena Rossi: Plus, which model. We currently use a mix. We can start with one.

[03:12] Simran Kaur: Yeah, pick one representative model + prompt set first. We can do “model A” for acceptance and then optionally test “model B” for cost later.

[03:22] Priyom Das: On models: we can propose two candidates based on your quality requirements. But for the benchmark, we should choose one and pin the version.

[03:30] Nadia Patel: Okay.

[03:31] Markus Klein: Let’s define the benchmark methodology. You mentioned “traffic replay.” Chris, what do you have in mind? Like replaying actual API calls or synthetic?

[03:40] Chris Dwyer: We can export request logs from our gateway. But we can’t share raw data outside. Internally we can replay against your endpoint. The ask is: we want the replay harness to preserve concurrency and timing—like the burst profile.

[03:55] Markus Klein: Great. That’s the right approach. If you can run replay from your infra, that’s best. We can provide a simple harness or guide.

[04:04] Simran Kaur: And if you prefer we can do a “sanitized dataset” approach where we replace sensitive fields but keep length and structure. But it sounds like you’d rather run it entirely on your side.

[04:13] Chris Dwyer: Correct. We’ll run it from our VPC.

[04:16] Elena Rossi: The only thing is we need deterministic settings—temperature, top-p—so outputs are comparable.

[04:22] Markus Klein: Yep. For latency we typically run with temperature 0 or low, and no tool calls unless needed. But if tool calling is in your real workload, we should keep it. Otherwise we’re measuring something else.

[04:35] Samir Khan: Tool calling is like 10% of cases maybe.

[04:39] Simran Kaur: We can include a mixed prompt set. Like 90% pure generation, 10% structured output or function call. Even if it’s a stub tool.

[04:48] Nadia Patel: Let’s do that. We don’t want a benchmark that looks great but doesn’t match reality.

[04:54] Priyom Das: Okay, so we’ll create a prompt pack with categories: summary, anomaly explanation, and maybe a tool-call “lookup” category.

[05:06] Elena Rossi: We can provide examples. We’ll strip PII.

[05:10] Markus Klein: Now metrics. We usually track:
- TTFT (time to first token)
- end-to-end completion latency
- p50 / p95 / p99
- throughput in tokens/sec or requests/min at given concurrency
- error rates: 429, 5xx, timeouts
- and cost per 1k tokens, if we’re comparing economics

[05:30] Chris Dwyer: We care about p95. p99 is nice but p95 is what our internal dashboards use.

[05:36] Nadia Patel: Yeah, and failures. Even small error rates create manual work.

[05:41] Markus Klein: Let’s define acceptance thresholds explicitly. What are you aiming for today? Even ballpark.

[05:49] Nadia Patel: For the interactive part: TTFT under 500 milliseconds at normal load. Full response… under, say, 6 seconds p95 for the median prompt.

[06:00] Elena Rossi: But for the long prompts, it’s going to be higher. We should scope it to a defined prompt length, right?

[06:06] Simran Kaur: Exactly. We’ll define buckets. Like input 0–1k, 1k–2.5k, 2.5k+. And we’ll report p95 per bucket.

[06:16] Chris Dwyer: Concurrency target: we want to test at 50 concurrent with bursts to 80 for a short window.

[06:24] Markus Klein: Great. Then acceptance could be “at 50 concurrent sustained for 30 minutes, p95 completion latency <= X for bucket 1 and <= Y for bucket 2, error rate <= Z.”

[06:36] Priyom Das: And to be clear, Dedicated means you’ll get predictable behavior at that load if we size correctly.

[06:43] Nadia Patel: Right. What do you need to size?

[06:46] Simran Kaur: We need the output length distribution and the concurrency pattern. Then we can propose an initial GPU pool. We can adjust after the first load run.

[06:56] Elena Rossi: Are you going to tune batching and caching?

[07:00] Markus Klein: Yes, within the bounds of your latency goals. Continuous batching is usually the big lever. Caching depends on prefix reuse. Do you have repeated prefixes?

[07:09] Elena Rossi: Some. We have a template system so the first 200-300 tokens are consistent.

[07:15] Simran Kaur: That’s good for prefix caching. But we should test with it both on and off to see if it changes tail behavior.

[07:23] Chris Dwyer: Just call out any warm cache assumptions. We don’t want “works if cache is warm.”

[07:29] Markus Klein: Totally. We’ll do cold start runs and warm runs. We’ll document it.

[07:35] Priyom Das: On acceptance thresholds, can we propose something and you confirm? I don’t want to force numbers live.

[07:41] Nadia Patel: Yes. Put it in a doc.

[07:44] Markus Klein: Here’s a strawman. Tell me if this is crazy:
- At 50 concurrent sustained for 30 minutes:
  - TTFT p95 <= 700ms
  - Completion latency p95 <= 6.5s for prompts with input <= 2k tokens and output <= 800 tokens
  - Error rate (5xx + timeouts) <= 0.5%
- At burst to 80 concurrent for 10 minutes:
  - Completion latency p95 degrades no more than 25% from sustained
  - Error rate <= 1%

[08:20] Chris Dwyer: The error rates sound right. The latency… maybe. We should also cap 429s. We don’t want rate limiting to hide failures.

[08:28] Simran Kaur: Right. In Dedicated you shouldn’t see 429s unless you exceed agreed QPS. We can treat 429 as failure for the benchmark.

[08:37] Nadia Patel: I like that. If it rate limits, it’s not meeting the goal.

[08:42] Elena Rossi: Can we include p95 for streaming time-to-first-token separately? Because if TTFT is good but then it stalls, the UI still feels broken.

[08:52] Markus Klein: Yep. We can track “inter-token latency” or stall events, but that can get complicated. Alternatively we track: time to first token and time to 50 tokens.

[09:03] Simran Kaur: Time to 50 tokens is a good proxy for early streaming smoothness.

[09:07] Chris Dwyer: Works.

[09:10] Priyom Das: Okay. Now measurement details: we should agree on what time window, and where metrics come from. Are you measuring client-side or server-side?

[09:21] Chris Dwyer: Client-side from our harness. We can also capture your request IDs to correlate.

[09:27] Markus Klein: Perfect. Redwood Console will show server-side as well. We can compare.

[09:33] Elena Rossi: We need to ensure the harness uses keep-alive and doesn’t introduce its own overhead.

[09:39] Simran Kaur: Yep. We’ll include guidance. Also: fixed region. You said us-east?

[09:45] Chris Dwyer: Yes, us-east. That’s where our workload sits.

[09:49] Priyom Das: Great.

[09:51] Nadia Patel: Security question: for the POC, do you store prompts?

[09:55] Markus Klein: By default, we don’t store raw prompts for longer than the configured retention for debugging, and for Dedicated we can set retention to zero or near-zero depending on your needs. We do log metadata: timing, token counts, errors.

[10:10] Simran Kaur: And we can enable redaction for certain fields if you send structured payloads.

[10:16] Chris Dwyer: For the POC we can use sanitized prompts. So retention is less scary. But we still want to keep it minimal.

[10:23] Priyom Das: Understood. We’ll configure minimal retention and document it.

[10:28] Samir Khan: Coming back to economics: are we measuring cost per request or token?

[10:33] Priyom Das: For Dedicated, it’s typically a monthly capacity price, but for the POC we can still estimate effective cost per 1k tokens based on utilization. Markus can help compute it from the run.

[10:45] Markus Klein: Yep, we’ll export total tokens, total GPU-hours during the window, and compute unit cost. But acceptance is primarily latency/reliability.

[10:55] Nadia Patel: Latency and reliability first. Cost second, but we still want a view.

[11:01] Markus Klein: Makes sense.

[11:03] Priyom Das: Now, case study. You mentioned if it’s successful, you’re open. I want to be respectful: we can keep it conditional and lightweight.

[11:12] Nadia Patel: We can do a public case study if the outcome is strong and if we can approve language. We’d probably be okay with “QuantaPay reduced p95 latency by X” type statements, but we won’t share volumes.

[11:26] Priyom Das: Totally fine. We can avoid absolute traffic numbers. We can talk in percentages and describe architecture at a high level.

[11:33] Elena Rossi: And not disclose model choice if that’s sensitive.

[11:36] Simran Kaur: We can say “a Redwood-hosted open model” or “a Redwood-verified model” instead of naming it. Or we can name it if you want—your call.

[11:44] Nadia Patel: Let’s keep model name internal for now.

[11:48] Priyom Das: Great. Also we typically do one reference call a quarter max. Does that sound okay?

[11:55] Nadia Patel: If it’s for serious prospects, yes. We’ll need guardrails.

[12:00] Priyom Das: We have a prep sheet and we’ll always pre-brief you on who, what they’re evaluating, and topics to avoid.

[12:07] Chris Dwyer: Cool.

[12:09] Markus Klein: Back to the technical plan—let’s outline the actual benchmark runs.

[12:14] Markus Klein: I propose:
1) Calibration run: 10–20 minutes at low concurrency, validate correctness, measure baseline lat.
2) Sustained run: 30 minutes at 50 concurrent, steady-state.
3) Burst run: 10 minutes ramping to 80 concurrent.
4) Soak run: 2 hours at 30 concurrent to catch slow degradation, memory issues.

[12:37] Chris Dwyer: I like the soak. We’ve seen memory fragmentation issues in our self-hosted vLLM setup.

[12:43] Simran Kaur: Yep, KV cache behavior over time matters.

[12:47] Elena Rossi: For correctness, what’s the validation? We can’t compare exact text because it’s probabilistic.

[12:54] Markus Klein: Right. We’ll do “schema validity” for structured output: parseable JSON, required keys present. And for free-form: basic checks like non-empty, no truncation, and maybe a lightweight evaluation on a sample set.

[13:09] Samir Khan: We can also do a human spot check from the risk team.

[13:13] Priyom Das: That’s perfect for sign-off.

[13:16] Chris Dwyer: Also, timeouts. We currently set 30 seconds. We should keep that.

[13:21] Simran Kaur: Yes. Keep your production timeout settings in the harness. That way failures map to real impact.

[13:28] Elena Rossi: For streaming, we use SSE. Does your endpoint support that?

[13:33] Markus Klein: Yes, streaming SSE. We’ll provide example code in Python and Node. The harness can either consume stream or measure time-to-first-byte.

[13:43] Chris Dwyer: We should consume it, because we’ve seen providers that start stream then stall.

[13:48] Markus Klein: Agreed.

[13:50] Priyom Das: Let me check: your current provider is OpenAI direct or through Bedrock?

[13:55] Nadia Patel: We’re on Bedrock for some, OpenAI for others. We’re trying to consolidate.

[14:02] Priyom Das: Okay, helpful context. In the case study we can say “previous managed LLM endpoints,” we don’t need to name them.

[14:09] Nadia Patel: Yes, please.

[14:12] Markus Klein: For comparison baseline, do you want to run the same harness against your current stack?

[14:18] Chris Dwyer: Yes, but we’ll do that internally. We can share deltas.

[14:22] Simran Kaur: Great. And we’ll provide a “metrics worksheet” so the deltas are computed consistently.

[14:28] Elena Rossi: Question on “Dedicated.” Is it a fixed set of GPUs or can it autoscale?

[14:35] Priyom Das: Dedicated is reserved capacity, but you can configure burst capacity options. For the POC we’ll likely keep it fixed to make results stable, and then we can model burst options.

[14:47] Markus Klein: For this benchmark, stability > fancy scaling. We can test a second config if you want.

[14:53] Chris Dwyer: Makes sense.

[14:55] Nadia Patel: What about rollout/fallback? If we have a latency incident, can it fall back to a smaller model?

[15:03] Simran Kaur: Yes, we can set policy-based routing and fallback. For POC, we should probably keep it simple: one model, one config. But we can do a demo of fallback.

[15:14] Markus Klein: And we can show how the Console would reflect it.

[15:18] Samir Khan: For now, the benchmark is primary. Fallback is nice-to-have.

[15:23] Priyom Das: Okay.

[15:25] Markus Klein: Elena, what about max tokens? Do you have a cap?

[15:28] Elena Rossi: We cap output at 900 tokens for this workflow.

[15:33] Markus Klein: Great. That makes it easier to bound performance.

[15:37] Chris Dwyer: One more thing: we’ve seen providers optimize for short outputs and then tail latency explodes for longer completions.

[15:45] Simran Kaur: Yep. That’s why we’ll report per bucket and include long cases explicitly.

[15:52] Markus Klein: We can also include a “worst-case” test: input 2k, output 900, 20 concurrency, just to see tail.

[16:01] Nadia Patel: Do it.

[16:03] Priyom Das: Sounds like we have alignment. Let’s talk deliverables and owners.

[16:09] Priyom Das: From Redwood, we’ll send a POC plan doc. Markus will include the benchmark definitions and Simran will propose capacity sizing once we have distributions.

[16:18] Elena Rossi: From our side, I’ll provide sanitized prompts and parameter settings, like temperature, top-p, tool calling mix.

[16:26] Chris Dwyer: I’ll own the replay harness and the load profiles. We use k6 sometimes, but for streaming it’s weird. Might do a custom Python.

[16:36] Markus Klein: Yeah, k6 + streaming SSE can be annoying. We can share a reference harness we’ve used.

[16:43] Simran Kaur: And if you want, we can join a working session to set it up.

[16:47] Nadia Patel: That would be helpful.

[16:50] Priyom Das: Great. Now, acceptance criteria—Nadia, who signs off? You? Or someone else?

[16:56] Nadia Patel: Ultimately me and Samir, with Elena confirming the model quality isn’t worse.

[17:04] Samir Khan: Yeah. If the risk reviewers say it’s “good enough” and latency meets targets, we proceed.

[17:10] Priyom Das: Perfect.

[17:12] Markus Klein: Quick detail: When we compute p95, we should define it as end-to-end client measured, including network. That’s what matters.

[17:21] Chris Dwyer: Agree.

[17:22] Markus Klein: We’ll also capture server-side to debug if there’s disagreement.

[17:28] Simran Kaur: Also we should agree on retry behavior. If your harness retries failures, it can hide error rates.

[17:35] Chris Dwyer: We won’t retry for the benchmark. We’ll log raw results.

[17:39] Markus Klein: Great.

[17:41] Priyom Das: Okay, last piece: case study conditional language. What’s comfortable? We can keep it to: “If benchmark meets agreed thresholds, QuantaPay will consider participating in a public case study and one reference call,” subject to approval.

[17:58] Nadia Patel: That works. “Consider” and “subject to approval” are key.

[18:02] Priyom Das: Yup.

[18:04] Markus Klein: And for the case study metrics, we’ll use the same benchmark window and define it clearly, so there’s no ambiguity.

[18:12] Elena Rossi: Also, please no mention of our fraud rates or anything. Just performance and ops outcomes.

[18:18] Priyom Das: Understood.

[18:20] (crosstalk)

[18:21] Simran Kaur: One question: do you require any specific compliance artifacts for the POC? Like SOC 2 report, pen test, etc.

[18:29] Chris Dwyer: Not for POC, but we’ll need SOC 2 before procurement.

[18:34] Priyom Das: We can provide SOC 2 under NDA. We’ll send it separately.

[18:39] Nadia Patel: Great.

[18:41] Markus Klein: Alright, I think we can recap next steps.

[18:45] Priyom Das: Recap:
1) Redwood sends POC plan + benchmark worksheet by tomorrow.
2) QuantaPay sends sanitized prompt set + length distribution + params by Monday.
3) We schedule a technical working session (Markus/Simran + Elena/Chris) early next week.
4) Redwood provisions Dedicated endpoint in us-east and pins model version.
5) We document acceptance thresholds and measurement windows in writing.

[19:12] Nadia Patel: Sounds good.

[19:14] Chris Dwyer: Works.

[19:15] Elena Rossi: Yep.

[19:17] Markus Klein: Great. Thanks all.

[19:20] Priyom Das: Thanks everyone.

(End of transcript)

Note: Fireflies transcript truncated some mid-call segments; remaining time included calendar holds / scheduling logistics and a short side discussion on test account setup and IP allowlisting.
